origin: Great Basin and Colorado Plateau — central Idaho and south-central Washington south to Utah, Nevada, Arizona and New Mexico
habitat: Dry, open or brushy alkaline valleys and foothills, often on volcanic soils and disturbed ground
blurb: The most intensely coloured of the globemallows — stiff wands crowded with small orange-to-brick-red cups above grey-white crinkled leaves shaped like a currant's. A true alkaline-soil desert plant, which is precisely why it is at home in Front Range clay.
water: Low; xeric — thrives on dry, lean ground with no supplemental water
spread: Clumping from a woody root crown; self-sows on open ground
seasons: Orange-red cups May–July along tall wands; grey crinkled foliage all season; dies back to the crown in winter
wildlife: Special value to native bees, including globemallow specialist bees

care.hardiness: A plant of cold high-desert valleys and foothills from Idaho and Washington south to Utah, Nevada and New Mexico, so it takes Front Range winters without trouble at zone 5b–6a. Heat and reflected glare are non-issues.[1][2]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into lean and sharply drained soil. It resents disturbance once its woody root is established, so plant young stock and leave it be. In pots, use a deep container and a gritty mineral mix kept dry.[2][1]
care.sun: Full sun. It grows in open, unshaded desert valleys and foothills; anything less and it leans and skimps on flowers.[1]
care.soil: Dry, well-draining, often volcanic or alkaline soil — the Wildflower Center's habitat note is literally 'alkaline valleys', which makes Boulder's high-pH ground an asset rather than an obstacle. Add grit to heavy clay; do not enrich it.[1][2]
care.water: Low. Genuinely xeric once established, as it is drought-adapted with deep roots. Summer irrigation aimed at neighbouring plants is the usual cause of death here, so site it away from a lawn or a drip zone.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space 18–24 in apart; the stems are upright and wandlike rather than bushy, so plant in threes for a fuller effect.[2]
care.propagation: By seed. The Wildflower Center notes the seeds display strong dormancy — the genus has a hard, water-impermeable coat — so scarify the seed before sowing, exactly as for Munro's globemallow. Established plants self-sow into bare ground.[1][2]
care.sow: Scarify, then sow in fall or very early spring so the seed gets natural chilling; sow shallowly on a lean, gritty surface. Untreated seed germinates poorly and unevenly.[1][2]
care.bloom: Orange to red cups, roughly May through July, ranged along the upper part of tall stems. Cutting spent wands back can bring a lighter second flush if there's late-summer moisture.[1]
care.maintenance: Very low. Cut old stems to the crown in late winter. Don't feed it and don't mulch it with compost — lean, dry, mineral soil is what keeps it compact and long-lived on the Front Range.[2][3]
care.selfsow: Self-sows on open, disturbed ground — it is a natural colonizer of disturbance in the wild. Deadhead before the capsules dry, or simply hoe off seedlings, if you want it to stay in place.[1][2]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases; the real risk is root and crown rot in wet or poorly drained ground. Like all globemallows it is clothed in fine stellate hairs that irritate skin and eyes, so wear gloves when handling it.[2][1]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use; a xeric ornamental whose fine star-shaped leaf hairs irritate skin and eyes.[1][2]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for gooseberryleaf globemallow, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it, and don't reason across from any other mallow. Despite the common name it is not a gooseberry and bears no edible fruit; the name describes the shape of its leaves. As with every globemallow, the fine stellate hairs covering the plant can irritate skin and especially eyes — wear gloves and keep your hands from your face when cutting it back.[1][2]
